title: US-Japan Joint Yen Intervention, Trump-Iran Diplomacy Clash, Europe's Rivers Hit Record Lows
subhead: The first US-Japan coordinated currency intervention since 2011 halts the yen's slide, while Trump and Tehran publicly contradict each other over the state of Hormuz negotiations, and drought chokes Europe's major waterways.

sections.heading: US and Japan Intervene Jointly to Prop Up the Yen
sections.body:
Japan and the United States confirmed on Monday that they carried out a rare joint currency intervention last week to halt a plunge in the yen that had pushed it to a 40-year low against the dollar. It is the first coordinated US-Japan forex action since 2011, when both countries acted after the Fukushima disaster.

Japan's Ministry of Finance said it sold nearly $59 billion worth of dollars on Thursday, before Friday's confirmed joint intervention with the US Treasury. A Reuters photograph of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's notepad during a Friday cabinet meeting read: 'To Do: Buy Japanese Yen $5-10 bil,' suggesting Washington's direct participation was sizable.

Bessent said the 'coordinated foreign exchange actions countered disorderly yen movements,' and Trump told reporters: 'They have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we're always there for Japan.' Both countries said they would not hesitate to conduct further joint interventions. The dollar fell to around 157 yen, well off the 164-yen peak from last month, according to the BBC and AP.

Oxford Economics' Shigeto Nagai said the US agreed to participate because it 'serves its national interests by offering the prospect of significant benefits at a low cost' — a stronger yen reduces Japanese export competitiveness pressure and could ease global financial instability that might push up US borrowing costs.
sections.whyItMatters: The first joint US-Japan currency action in 15 years signals that the dollar-yen imbalance had reached a threshold where Washington saw systemic risk. It also reflects deepening economic interdependence at a time when the Iran war is already disrupting global energy markets.

sections.heading: Trump and Iran Contradict Each Other Over Hormuz Talks
sections.body:
President Trump said on Sunday he had called off 'the biggest attack since World War II' on Iran after Gulf allies — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar — urged him to give diplomacy a chance. He declared that new negotiations would begin on Monday and that this was Iran's 'last chance' to reach a deal, insisting 'they're going on right now.'

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei directly contradicted this account, saying Tehran was not negotiating with the United States and was instead holding talks with Oman focused on establishing a temporary safe-passage route through the Strait of Hormuz. 'As long as the maritime siege and US actions continue, nothing significant will change in the Strait of Hormuz,' Baqaei said.

Trump responded by calling Iran's leadership 'unbelievably duplicitous' on Truth Social, while also referring to the US naval blockade as a 'Wall of Steel' and stating: 'Nothing gets through to Iran, unless we want it to, and nothing will get through, unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished.'

The gap between the two sides' public positions is wide. According to Kpler data, only eight vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday and 11 on Saturday — compared with more than 100 per day before the war. Iran's trade minister traveled to Pakistan on Monday to discuss routing Iranian container traffic through Pakistani ports as a workaround to the blockade, Al Jazeera reported.
sections.whyItMatters: The public contradiction between Washington and Tehran over whether negotiations are happening at all underscores how far apart the two sides remain. With Hormuz traffic at a fraction of pre-war levels and no diplomatic breakthrough in sight, the stalemate continues to squeeze global oil supplies.

sections.heading: Europe's Rivers Hit Record Lows as Heatwave Deepens Drought
sections.body:
The Rhine fell to its lowest recorded levels at measuring stations in Cologne and Lobith, on the German-Dutch border, last week, while Italy's Po River hit a historic low near Cremona. Germany's NIWIS system reported that 44% of Rhine stations and 78% of Danube stations registered 'extremely low' water levels at the end of July, the BBC reported.

The navigable water depth at the key Kaub chokepoint near Koblenz hit the 2018 record low of 25cm on Friday, forcing cargo vessels to lighten loads and spread freight across more ships — raising costs and threatening supply bottlenecks. The Rhine Waterways and Shipping Authority warned that shipping is unlikely to be suspended entirely but that precautions would be needed.

Power generation is also affected. Serbia cut output at coal plants due to cooling water shortages, while Romania carried out a controlled explosion on a Danube riverbank rock to maintain water flow to the Cernavoda nuclear plant. Two Romanian car factories — Dacia and Ford — agreed to halt production for more than two weeks to reduce electricity consumption.

Italy raised its drought alert to 'high' across the entire Po Valley, where saltwater intrusion from the sea is damaging farmland. Scientists at World Weather Attribution found that while there is no clear long-term rainfall decline, human-caused climate change is increasing evaporation and making drought conditions more likely.
sections.whyItMatters: The simultaneous record lows across multiple European river systems are disrupting shipping, power generation, and agriculture at a time when the Hormuz crisis is already straining energy logistics. The compounding effect of drought on top of conflict-driven supply shocks raises the risk of energy and food price inflation across the continent.

sections.heading: Ukrainian Drone Kills Seven on Russian Beach as Deep Strikes Continue
sections.body:
A Ukrainian drone hit a popular beach near the village of Arkhipo-Osipovka on Russia's Black Sea coast on Monday, killing seven people including three children and injuring 40, according to local authorities. BBC-verified video showed the drone hurtling toward a cliffside before crashing in a fireball near tourists.

It remains unclear whether the drone was shot down by air defences or jammed by electronic warfare. Several eyewitnesses told Russian media they heard gunfire before the explosion, suggesting an attempt to intercept it. No air-raid sirens sounded before the strike.

The attack came as Ukraine's long-range drone campaign against Russian territory continues to escalate. Overnight, a Ukrainian strike hit a Wildberries warehouse in the Vladimir region, east of Moscow — the latest in a string of attacks on the online retailer's facilities. Kyiv says Wildberries depots are used to supply the Russian military. Russia, for its part, killed at least nine people in a Saturday ballistic missile strike on Kyiv, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, destroying a residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district.

Russian anti-war politician Boris Nadezhdin announced Monday that he has fled Russia after being designated a 'foreign agent' last month. He posted a video from in front of the Eiffel Tower in Paris, saying: 'I'm alive and free. Unfortunately, I'm not in Russia at the moment.'
sections.whyItMatters: The beach strike underscores the human cost of Ukraine's deep-strike campaign and the vulnerability of Russian civilian areas near the front. Meanwhile, Nadezhdin's exile eliminates one of the last visible opposition figures inside Russia, further consolidating the Kremlin's domestic control ahead of September's Duma elections.

sections.heading: EU Demands Stronger Borders After Ceuta Crisis, 800 Minors Stranded
sections.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for 'united action' on border security after the mass crossing of roughly 60,000 migrants into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta last week. Spain now estimates 69,500 people have returned to Morocco, while the official death toll stands at 72 on the Spanish side and 11 on the Moroccan side.

Von der Leyen praised Spain's 'swift handling' but said Europe must 'double down' on preventing irregular migration, strengthening external borders, implementing early warning systems, dismantling smuggling networks, and reinforcing returns. EU interior ministers will hold emergency talks by video conference on Tuesday.

The crisis has divided the EU. Italy temporarily suspended its Schengen arrangement with Spain, with Finland and Denmark backing the move. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for Spain's Schengen membership to be temporarily suspended. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez accused some European governments of attacking Spain 'driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest,' pointing out that Ceuta is not part of the Schengen area.

Meanwhile, more than 800 unaccompanied minors remain stranded in Ceuta with limited food and shelter. Al Jazeera reported that a 17-year-old girl from Tangier saw her eight-year-old brother's body pulled from the sea during the crossing. Spain's only migrant centre in Ceuta has capacity for 600 people.
sections.whyItMatters: The Ceuta crisis is rapidly becoming a test case for whether the EU can maintain solidarity under pressure. Italy's Schengen suspension sets a precedent that could fragment free movement, while the plight of hundreds of unaccompanied children highlights the humanitarian gap in Europe's border response.

sections.heading: Pentagon Awards $58 Billion Patriot Contract as Missile Stockpiles Strain
sections.body:
The US Department of Defense announced a major deal with Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman to accelerate production of Patriot PAC-3 and THAAD missile interceptor systems. Lockheed received a seven-year contract worth more than $58 billion — converting a previous one-year, $4.7 billion contract — while Northrop Grumman's share exceeds $3 billion.

The deal will triple Patriot production and quadruple THAAD output, according to Al Jazeera. Undersecretary of War Michael Duffey called it part of building the 'Arsenal of Freedom.' Northrop Grumman said investments made in 2021 had already nearly tripled production capacity at its Allegany Ballistics Laboratory in West Virginia.

The acceleration comes as US missile stockpiles face strain from simultaneous commitments in the Iran conflict, continued military assistance to Ukraine — which is running low on Patriot interceptors, its only defence against ballistic missiles — and deployments across the Gulf.
sections.whyItMatters: The scale of the contract — $58 billion over seven years — reflects how seriously the Pentagon takes the depletion of its interceptor inventory across multiple active theaters. It also signals to allies and adversaries alike that the US intends to sustain high-tempo air defence operations for years to come.

bottomLine: The first joint US-Japan currency intervention since 2011 arrested the yen's collapse and signalled Washington's willingness to stabilise allied economies amid the broader disruption of the Iran war. But the day's defining feature is the public diplomatic gap between Washington and Tehran: Trump claims negotiations are underway, Iran denies it, and Hormuz traffic remains at a trickle. Meanwhile, Europe faces simultaneous strain from record drought choking its rivers and a migration crisis testing its unity, while the Pentagon's $58 billion interceptor contract underscores that the military dimensions of the current global instability show no signs of easing.
